title: Self-constructed automated syringe for preparation of micron-sized particulate samples in x-ray microtomography
author: Ditscherlein, Leißner, et al.

steps.title: Gather materials and equipment
steps.instruction: Collect all reagents, consumables and hardware required for the preparation of wax‑embedded particulate samples and for building the automated syringe.

substeps.instruction: Histological wax (Poth‑Hille, product code PHC9061) with a melting point of 59 °C to 61 °C.
Silicone tube with an inner diameter of 2 mm (the required sample size for the ZEISS Xradia VERSA 510 tomographic measurements).
Soda‑lime glass particles (SiLibeads, type S, Sigmund Lindner) with diameters below 50 µm; composition 72.3 % SiO2, 13.3 % Na2O, 8.9 % CaO, 4.0 % MgO, 1.5 % other oxides.
LEGO parts listed in Table 1 (exact brick names, quantities and part numbers).
Arduino UNO R3 board, NXT‑Shield, LEGO NXT motors and sensors, and a Wayne & Lane circuit board for connecting the Arduino to the LEGO components.
Heating gun for melting wax.
Extraction rack with a mounted validation sample (as shown in Fig. 2).
Commercial syringe reference: standard infusion syringes start at ≈ 1300 €, dual‑function syringes at ≈ 2300 €, the present low‑cost design reduces cost by a factor of 10–15.
X‑ray micro‑tomography system: ZEISS Xradia VERSA 510, 2048‑pixel detector, camera binning 2, operating at 80 keV and 7 W.

steps.title: Assemble the automated syringe
steps.instruction: Build the syringe mounting, tube connector and rack from the LEGO parts and integrate the electronics.

substeps.instruction: Use the LEGO Digital Designer files (supplemental material) to construct the mounting shown in Fig. 3A and the 3‑D model in Fig. 3B.
Attach the syringe (b) to the LEGO mounting (a) and connect the silicone tube (a) to the tube connector (c).
Mount the Arduino UNO R3 on the assembly, connect the NXT‑Shield and wire the LEGO NXT motors and trigger to the Wayne & Lane circuit board.

Upload the provided Arduino script (supplemental material) to the board; the script defines a controlled start‑up to avoid abrupt motion and sets the translation speed v that converts the gear rotation into piston movement.
Verify that the high‑torque NXT motors can move the piston smoothly with low Arduino voltages.

steps.title: Melt the wax
steps.instruction: Heat the histological wax above its melting point to obtain a liquid matrix.

substeps.instruction: Set the heating gun to a temperature ≥ 61 °C (just above the wax melting range of 59–61 °C).
Melt the required amount of wax until it becomes a clear liquid.

steps.title: Load particles into the silicone tube
steps.instruction: Introduce the particulate sample into the tube before embedding.

substeps.instruction: Insert the soda‑lime glass beads (size < 50 µm) into the 2 mm‑ID silicone tube.
Adjust the particle concentration to the target values used for validation (e.g., 10 % or 15 % as listed in Table 2).

steps.title: Embed particles in molten wax
steps.instruction: Fill the tube with liquid wax to suspend the particles.

substeps.instruction: Using a pipette or the assembled syringe, inject the molten wax into the silicone tube until the particles are fully immersed.
Avoid air bubbles; ensure a homogeneous distribution of particles within the wax.

steps.title: Shock‑freeze the wax matrix
steps.instruction: Rapidly solidify the wax to prevent particle segregation.

substeps.instruction: Immediately after filling, place the tube in a cold environment (e.g., ice‑salt bath) to freeze the wax quickly (shock freezing).
Confirm that the wax has solidified completely before proceeding.

steps.title: Extract sub‑samples with the automated syringe
steps.instruction: Withdraw defined volumes from specific heights of the solidified wax tube.

substeps.instruction: Mount the frozen wax tube on the extraction rack (Fig. 2A).
Program the syringe to move the piston with a dynamic suction volume V, converting gear rotation to linear translation at speed v (as defined in the Arduino script).
Extract three sub‑samples from the top, middle and bottom positions of the tube (Fig. 2C).
Collect each sub‑sample in a separate container for subsequent imaging.

steps.title: Perform X‑ray micro‑tomography
steps.instruction: Scan the extracted sub‑samples using the ZEISS Xradia VERSA 510 system under the required geometrical conditions.

substeps.instruction: Place each sub‑sample in the scanner ensuring rotational symmetry and that the sample fits the field of view (FOV) to avoid artefacts.
Acquire tomographic data with the detector settings: 2048 pixels, camera binning 2, 80 keV, 7 W.

steps.title: Analyze particle size distribution
steps.instruction: Process the tomographic data to obtain number‑based cumulative distributions and quantiles.

substeps.instruction: Segment individual particles in the 3‑D volume, avoiding over‑segmentation and under‑segmentation.
Calculate the equivalent spherical diameter (ESD) for each particle.
Generate cumulative distribution curves and box‑plots for the top, middle and bottom extraction points (as shown in Fig. 5).
Compare the results with the reference data in Table 2 (average, standard deviation, quantiles for each extraction height).

steps.title: Record all experimental parameters
steps.instruction: Document every numeric detail of the experiment for reproducibility.

substeps.instruction: Wax melting point: 59–61 °C.
Silicone tube inner diameter: 2 mm.
Particle size range: < 50 µm.
Particle composition: 72.3 % SiO2, 13.3 % Na2O, 8.9 % CaO, 4.0 % MgO, 1.5 % others.
X‑ray system: ZEISS Xradia VERSA 510, 2048‑pixel detector, binning 2, 80 keV, 7 W.
Commercial syringe cost reference: ≈ 1300 € (infusion only), ≈ 2300 € (dual), cost reduction factor 10–15 for the LEGO‑based design.
LEGO part list as in Table 1 (all part numbers and quantities).
Extraction heights and target concentrations as in Table 2 (e.g., 10 % and 15 % concentrations, average particle numbers per experiment).

description: New application fields of particle technology, e.g. coatings, pharmaceuticals or electronic components require more and more highly defined particles in the lower micrometer range. In this case, the particle size distribution (PSD) is no longer sufficient to define the specifications alone. The particle system has to be described by the PSD, but also by further distributed properties, which are for instance the particle shape distribution or the particle composition distribution. Tomographic particle characterization is one key methodology to provide the data, required to quantify these specifications. The tomogram of a representative particle sample contains information on the size and shape of each individual particle. The data of X-ray absorption furthermore gives hints on the material properties and structure of intergrown or composite structures. One central task in the tomography of a particle sample is the segmentation of the image data. When the particles in the sample are too close to each other, separating individuals can be challenging (one possible approach for segmentation algorithms for aggregated particles is given by Münch et al. [2]). On the other hand, oversegmentation can occur, when a particle is separated into two or more individuals during the image processing. In both cases, the physical sample preparation, which keeps the particles at a defined distance, is a key factor to minimize image segmentation errors. The established techniques known from SEM, TEM or automated mineralogy (MLA) cannot be transferred to X-ray tomography, because they only have to provide a representative 2D-measuring plane. The 3D-sample preparation introduced here, is able to provide a homogeneous particle sample immobilized (minimization of segregation and agglomeration: Fig. 1-A, B) within a matrix material with low X-ray absorption that fits the required geometrical demands.
